topics.title: Space lattice, unit cell, crystal systems
BCC / FCC / HCP: numbers, APF, a–R relations

questions.text: A space lattice is an infinite 3-D array of points in which:

options.label: d
options.text: the array cannot be generated by translation

questions.keyExplanation: Definition: every lattice point has identical surroundings.
questions.concise: A space lattice is an infinite 3-D array where every point has identical surroundings.
questions.detailed:
The defining property of a Bravais lattice is that the environment (number, type and
arrangement of neighbours) around every lattice point is identical. Translation by any lattice
vector maps the whole lattice onto itself.
- (b) Points are randomly arranged → that is an *amorphous* solid, not a lattice.
- (c) Only corner points are equivalent → *all* points are equivalent by definition.
- (d) Cannot be generated by translation → the opposite of the truth; a lattice is *defined* by
  translational periodicity.

questions.text: The unit cell is:

options.label: a
options.text: the largest group of atoms in a crystal

options.label: b
options.text: the smallest group of atoms which, repeated in 3-D by translation, reproduces the whole crystal

options.label: c
options.text: any group of atoms chosen at random

options.label: d
options.text: the group of atoms with the highest symmetry only

questions.keyExplanation: Smallest repeating group that regenerates the whole crystal by translation.
questions.concise: The unit cell is the smallest repeating brick that regenerates the crystal.
questions.detailed:
By definition the unit cell is the smallest parallelepiped which, stacked by pure
translation in three dimensions, builds the entire crystal.
- (a) "Largest group" is wrong — it is the *smallest* repeating group.
- (c) "Any group chosen at random" cannot guarantee reproduction of the crystal.
- (d) "The group with the highest symmetry only" is too restrictive — the *conventional* unit
  cell is often chosen for symmetry, but that is a convention, not the definition.

questions.text: The number of independent lattice parameters needed to fully describe a unit cell is:
questions.keyExplanation: Six parameters: a, b, c and α, β, γ.
questions.concise: Six lattice parameters: a, b, c (lengths) and α, β, γ (angles).
questions.detailed:
A unit cell is fully described by three edge lengths and the three angles between them:
```
lengths:  a, b, c
angles:   α (between b and c), β (between a and c), γ (between a and b)
```
That is 6 independent parameters. The 7 crystal systems differ only in which of these are
constrained equal or 90° (see Q6).

questions.text: The total number of Bravais lattices in three dimensions is:
questions.keyExplanation: 7 crystal systems → 14 Bravais lattices.
questions.concise: 7 crystal systems → 14 Bravais lattices.
questions.detailed:
There are 7 crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, rhombohedral,
monoclinic, triclinic), and allowing the different lattice-centring choices (P, I, F, C) gives
**14 Bravais lattices** in three dimensions.
- (a) 3 is the number of *centred* lattice types or the number of dimensions.
- (b) 7 is the number of *crystal systems*, not Bravais lattices.
- (d) 32 is the number of crystal *point groups*.
The 7-vs-14 distinction is a favourite quick-recall exam item.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true of the *unit cell*?

statements.text: It is the smallest repeating parallelepiped.
One valid description is the smallest atom group possessing the full crystal properties.
Its faces are parallel and opposite.
It may be defined by the orientation relationship of neighbouring cells.

questions.keyExplanation: All four are valid textbook descriptions — classic [P1]. Ask "could more than one be true?" before picking a single one.
questions.concise: All four are valid textbook descriptions of the unit cell.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the smallest repeating parallelepiped.
- Item 2 — TRUE: a second valid definition — the smallest atom group possessing the full crystal properties.
- Item 3 — TRUE: opposite faces are parallel and identical.
- Item 4 — TRUE: its orientation defines the orientation of the whole crystal (relevant to
  single-crystal growth and to texture/anisotropy in Ch. 2 §2.6).

Because all four can be true at once, this is a genuine "all are correct" case. Your Quiz I
correction identified this as failure pattern P1 — before committing to one option, ask
"could more than one of these be true?" and check for an all-inclusive option.

questions.text: A crystal has a = b ≠ c and α = β = 90°, γ = 120°. It belongs to which system?
questions.keyExplanation: a = b ≠ c, α = β = 90°, γ = 120° is the hexagonal signature.
questions.concise: a = b ≠ c, α = β = 90°, γ = 120° is the hexagonal signature.
questions.detailed:
Matching the constraints to the crystal systems:
| System | Signature |
|---|---|
| Tetragonal | a = b ≠ c, α = β = γ = 90° |
| **Hexagonal** | **a = b ≠ c, α = β = 90°, γ = 120°** |
| Orthorhombic | a ≠ b ≠ c, α = β = γ = 90° |
| Rhombohedral | a = b = c, α = β = γ ≠ 90° |

The distinguishing clue here is **γ = 120°** — that single non-right angle (with two equal
in-plane lengths) is unique to the hexagonal system.

questions.text: The number of atoms per unit cell in BCC, FCC and HCP respectively is:
questions.keyExplanation: BCC 2, FCC 4, HCP 6.
questions.concise: BCC 2, FCC 4, HCP 6 atoms per unit cell.
questions.detailed:
```
BCC: 8 corners × 1/8 + 1 body-centre = 1 + 1 = 2
FCC: 8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2  = 1 + 3 = 4
HCP: 12 corners × 1/6 + 2 faces × 1/2 + 3 internal = 2 + 1 + 3 = 6
```
(The HCP cell has 3 fully-internal atoms.) These three numbers — 2, 4, 6 — are worth
memorising as a set; they drive the APF and density calculations.

questions.text: The coordination numbers of BCC, FCC and HCP respectively are:
questions.keyExplanation: BCC 8; FCC 12; HCP 12 (max possible).
questions.concise: BCC 8; FCC 12; HCP 12 (the maximum possible for equal spheres).
questions.detailed:
- BCC — each atom has 8 nearest neighbours (the body-centre atom touches all 8 corners).
- FCC — 12 nearest neighbours in the close-packed plane and adjacent layers.
- HCP — also 12 (ideal c/a), the maximum packing coordination for equal hard spheres.

The key contrast: **BCC has coordination number 8, not 12.** FCC and HCP share CN 12 —
that equality is exactly why they share APF 0.74 (see Q9).

questions.text: The atomic packing factors of BCC, FCC and HCP respectively are:
questions.keyExplanation: 0.68 / 0.74 / 0.74 — the fastest sanity check before an exam.
questions.detailed:
```
APF = (number of atoms × volume of one atom) / volume of unit cell

BCC: n = 2, a = 4R/√3
     APF = 2 × (4/3)πR³ / (4R/√3)³ = π√3/8 ≈ 0.68

FCC: n = 4, a = 2√2 R
     APF = 4 × (4/3)πR³ / (2√2R)³ = π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74

HCP: ideal (c/a = 1.633) → APF = π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74 (same as FCC)
```
So BCC (0.68) is *not* close-packed; FCC and HCP tie at the close-packed limit of 0.74.
The APF triple 0.68 / 0.74 / 0.74 is the single fastest sanity-check in the chapter.

questions.text: In BCC, atoms touch along the:
questions.keyExplanation: Body diagonal √3 a = 4R.
questions.concise: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal: √3 a = 4R.
questions.detailed:
BCC has no atoms on the faces, so there is no face contact. The only line along
which atoms actually touch is the **body diagonal**, where one atom sits at each corner and one
at the body centre:
```
body diagonal length = √3 a
this spans 4 atomic radii (R + 2R + R)
⇒ √3 a = 4R  ⇒  a = 4R/√3
```
- (a) Atoms do *not* touch along the cube edge in BCC (there is a gap).
- (b) Face diagonal has no touching atoms in BCC.

questions.text: In FCC, atoms touch along the:
questions.keyExplanation: Face diagonal √2 a = 4R.
questions.concise: In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal: √2 a = 4R.
questions.detailed:
FCC has atoms at each face centre which touch the four corner atoms of that face:
```
face diagonal length = √2 a
this spans 4 atomic radii
⇒ √2 a = 4R  ⇒  a = 4R/√2 = 2√2 R
```
- (a) Atoms do *not* touch along the cube edge in FCC.
- (c) The body diagonal has no touching atoms in FCC (unlike BCC).
This BCC/FCC "which diagonal?" contrast is a classic exam discriminator — pair it with Q10.

questions.text: For BCC with atomic radius R, the lattice parameter a equals:
questions.concise: BCC: a = 4R/√3.
questions.detailed:
From Q10, atoms touch along the body diagonal:
```
√3 a = 4R  ⇒  a = 4R/√3 ≈ 2.309 R
```
- (a) 2R is the HCP/SC relation (a = 2R).
- (b) 2√2 R is the FCC relation.
- (d) 4R/√2 is a confused form of the FCC relation.

questions.text: For FCC with atomic radius R, the lattice parameter a equals:
questions.detailed:
From Q11, atoms touch along the face diagonal:
```
√2 a = 4R  ⇒  a = 4R/√2 = 2√2 R ≈ 2.828 R
```
- (a) 2R is HCP/SC.
- (c) 4R/√3 is BCC.
- (d) 4R is meaningless here.
Note 4R/√2 and 2√2 R are the *same* number — if both appear in an option set, they are not
distinct answers.

questions.text: The BCC structure has *lower* packing efficiency (0.68) than FCC/HCP (~0.74). Which statement(s) correctly follow(s)?

statements.text: BCC is not close-packed.
BCC has fewer close-packed slip systems than FCC.
BCC metals are generally less ductile and more prone to a ductile–brittle transition.
BCC has a coordination number of 12.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1–3 follow from 0.68 packing. Item 4 is **false** (BCC CN = 8). [P2] — the FCC/HCP pair has CN 12.
questions.concise: BCC is not close-packed (0.68), has fewer easy slip systems, and tends to be less ductile — but its CN is 8, not 12.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: APF 0.68 < 0.74, so BCC is not close-packed.
- Item 2 — TRUE: BCC's {110}⟨111⟩ is not a true close-packed system (no truly close-packed
  plane), and it is less readily activated than FCC's {111}⟨110⟩.
- Item 3 — TRUE: this is why BCC metals (α-Fe, Cr, W) show a ductile–brittle transition and
  are generally less ductile at low temperature.
- Item 4 — FALSE: BCC's coordination number is **8**, not 12. CN 12 belongs to FCC and HCP.

This is a [P2] paired-terminology trap: the number 12 is *true of the sibling structure*
(FCC/HCP) and has been transplanted onto BCC.

questions.text: Which of the following metals has the FCC structure at room temperature?
questions.keyExplanation: Al is FCC. α-Fe, Cr, W are BCC.
questions.concise: Aluminium is FCC at room temperature.
questions.detailed:
FCC metals at room temperature include **γ-Fe, Al, Cu, Ni, Ag, Au, Pb**.
- (a) α-Fe is **BCC**.
- (b) Cr is **BCC**.
- (d) W is **BCC**.
Note the iron-specific trap: it is *γ*-Fe that is FCC, not α-Fe (see Q46).

questions.text: Which of the following has the BCC structure at room temperature?
questions.keyExplanation: V (vanadium) is BCC. Cu is FCC, γ-Fe is FCC, Mg is HCP.
questions.concise: Vanadium is BCC; Cu/γ-Fe are FCC, Mg is HCP.
questions.detailed:
BCC metals at room temperature include **α-Fe, Cr, W, Mo, V, Nb**.
- (a) Cu is **FCC**.
- (b) γ-Fe is **FCC** (only α-Fe and δ-Fe are BCC).
- (c) Mg is **HCP**.
- (d) V (vanadium) is **BCC** ✓

questions.text: Which of the following has the HCP structure?
questions.keyExplanation: Zn is HCP. Ni/Ag/Pb are FCC.
questions.concise: Zn is HCP; Ni, Ag, Pb are FCC.
questions.detailed:
HCP metals include **Zn, Mg, Ti, Co, Be**.
- (a) Ni — FCC, (b) Ag — FCC, (d) Pb — FCC.
If you can list three or four examples of each structure, most "which has structure X" questions
become instant recall.

questions.text: The HCP stacking sequence is:
questions.keyExplanation: HCP = ABAB… [P2] vs FCC's ABCABC…
questions.concise: HCP stacks ABAB…; this is the [P2] counterpart of FCC's ABCABC….
questions.detailed:
In HCP the close-packed {0001} basal layers repeat every *two* layers:
```
A B A B A B …
```
Only two distinct layer positions are needed, because the third layer sits directly above the
first. Contrast FCC (Q19), which needs three.
If you can picture the two stacking sequences, you can also explain *why* HCP has only one
close-packed plane while FCC has four.

questions.text: The FCC stacking sequence on {111} planes is:
questions.keyExplanation: FCC {111} close-packed planes stack ABCABC…
questions.concise: FCC {111} close-packed planes stack ABCABC….
questions.detailed:
In FCC the third close-packed layer sits in a *third* distinct position, giving:
```
A B C A B C …
```
This needs three distinct layer positions and is what defines the four equivalent {111}
close-packed planes. Q18 and Q19 are the canonical [P2] pair — say both sequences out loud
once and you will not mix them again.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the FCC/HCP packing factor of 0.74 is/are correct?

statements.text: It is a hard geometric ceiling — no arrangement of equal spheres packs denser.
FCC and HCP have identical packing density, differing only in stacking order.
This equality of packing density is why FCC and HCP metals have identical ductility.
FCC has four equivalent close-packed {111} planes to slip on; HCP has effectively only one basal plane.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 4 correct. Item 3 is **false** — identical packing density does *not* give identical ductility (FCC has 4 close-packed planes, HCP has 1). [P2]
questions.concise: 0.74 is the hard packing ceiling and FCC/HCP tie on it — but identical packing does *not* mean identical ductility.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: no arrangement of equal spheres packs denser than 0.74.
- Item 2 — TRUE: FCC and HCP have identical packing density; only the stacking order differs.
- Item 3 — FALSE: identical packing density does **not** give identical ductility. FCC has four
  equivalent {111} close-packed planes; HCP has effectively one basal plane. This is the [P2] trap.
- Item 4 — TRUE: FCC 4 close-packed planes vs HCP's effectively one.

This is the single most important conceptual point linking Ch. 2 to Ch. 6: the packing is the
same, the *slip-system count* is not, and ductility follows the slip systems.

questions.text: The ideal axial ratio c/a for HCP is:
questions.keyExplanation: Ideal c/a = 1.633 for perfect hard-sphere packing.
questions.concise: Ideal HCP c/a = √(8/3) ≈ 1.633.
questions.detailed:
For perfect hard-sphere packing in HCP, the axial ratio is fixed by geometry:
```
c/a = √(8/3) = 1.633
```
- (a) 1.414 = √2 (FCC face-diagonal factor).
- (c) 1.732 = √3 (BCC body-diagonal factor).
- (d) 1.860 is *zinc's* real value (see Q22), not the ideal.
Note your Ch. 2 notes flag that 1.633 also appears as d₁₁₁(FCC) and d₁₁₀(BCC) in units of R —
same number, unrelated origin (see Q33/Q34).

questions.text: Real HCP metals deviate from the ideal c/a = 1.633. Which set is correct?
questions.keyExplanation: Zn stretched (1.86 > 1.633); Ti compressed (1.59 < 1.633).
questions.concise: Zn is stretched (c/a > 1.633); Ti is compressed (c/a < 1.633).
questions.detailed:
```
Zn: c/a ≈ 1.86  > 1.633  →  stretched along c
Ti: c/a ≈ 1.59  < 1.633  →  compressed along c
```
Real HCP metals deviate from the ideal because their bonding is not perfectly isotropic
hard-sphere packing. Knowing *which direction* each deviates (rather than just the numbers)
lets you reason about which slip systems are favoured.

questions.text: Crystallographic directions are enclosed in:
questions.keyExplanation: Directions [uvw]; planes (hkl); families {hkl} or ⟨uvw⟩.
questions.concise: Directions use square brackets [uvw].
questions.detailed:
The notation convention:
```
[uvw]   →  one specific direction
⟨uvw⟩   →  a family of equivalent directions
(hkl)   →  one specific plane
{hkl}   →  a family of equivalent planes
```
Round brackets and braces are for *planes*, not single directions.

questions.text: A family of equivalent *directions* is written:
questions.keyExplanation: ⟨uvw⟩ is the direction *family*.
questions.concise: Angle brackets ⟨uvw⟩ denote a direction family.
questions.detailed:
⟨uvw⟩ is the *family* of all directions related by the crystal's symmetry (e.g.
⟨110⟩ in cubic includes [110], [101], [011] and their negatives). Square brackets [uvw] (Q23)
denote one specific direction. Braces {hkl} (Q25) are for plane *families*. Three notations,
three meanings — a favourite [P2] discriminator.

questions.text: A family of equivalent *planes* is written:
questions.keyExplanation: {hkl} is the plane *family*. [P2] — brackets vs braces.
questions.concise: Braces {hkl} denote a plane family.
questions.detailed:
{hkl} collects all symmetry-equivalent planes (in cubic, {111} = (111), (11̄1),
(111̄), (1̄11) and the opposites — four distinct planes). Parentheses (hkl) denote one specific
parallel set. This is the mirror of Q24 and the same [P2] family.

questions.text: To obtain Miller indices (hkl) for a plane, the correct procedure is:

options.label: a
options.text: take intercepts, take reciprocals, clear fractions

options.label: b
options.text: take reciprocals, take intercepts, clear fractions

options.label: c
options.text: take intercepts, reduce to smallest integers directly

options.label: d
options.text: take Miller indices of the normal to the plane, then invert

questions.keyExplanation: Intercepts → reciprocals → clear fractions.
questions.concise: Intercepts → reciprocals → clear fractions.
questions.detailed:
The standard three-step procedure:
```
1. Find where the plane cuts the axes (intercepts), using ∞ if parallel.
2. Take the reciprocal of each intercept.
3. Clear any fractions to the smallest integers; enclose in (hkl).
```
- (b) reverses steps 1 and 2.
- (c) reduces intercepts directly instead of taking reciprocals — this is the classic error that
  produces a *mirrored* index (see Q28/Q29).
- (d) inverts the normal — not the procedure.
**Why reciprocals?** So that a plane parallel to an axis (intercept ∞) gets index 0, which is
convenient.

questions.text: A plane is parallel to x and y, and cuts z at −1. Its Miller indices are:
questions.keyExplanation: Parallel to x,y → indices 0,0; cut z at −1 → reciprocal −1 → (001̄).
questions.concise: Parallel to x and y → 0, 0; cuts z at −1 → reciprocal −1 → (001̄).
questions.detailed:
```
Intercepts:  x = ∞,  y = ∞,  z = −1
Reciprocals: 1/∞ = 0,  1/∞ = 0,  1/(−1) = −1
Indices:     (0 0 1̄)   →  written (001̄)
```
The bar over the 1 denotes the negative intercept. This plane is the top (or bottom) face of
the cell, flipped.

questions.text: A plane cuts x at ½, is parallel to y, and cuts z at 1. Its Miller indices are:
questions.keyExplanation: Intercepts ½, ∞, 1 → reciprocals 2, 0, 1 → (201).
questions.concise: Intercepts ½, ∞, 1 → reciprocals 2, 0, 1 → (201).
questions.detailed:
```
Intercepts:  x = ½,  y = ∞,  z = 1
Reciprocals: 1/½ = 2,  1/∞ = 0,  1/1 = 1
Indices:     (2 0 1)  →  (201)
```
Note the first index is **2**, not 1 — a small intercept gives a *large* index (see Q29). If you
reduced the intercepts directly instead of taking reciprocals you would wrongly get (101).

questions.text: Why does (201) have a larger first index than (100)?

options.label: a
options.text: because (201) has a *smaller* intercept on x, and indices are reciprocals of intercepts

options.label: b
options.text: because (201) has a *larger* intercept on x

options.label: d
options.text: because indices are not related to intercepts

questions.keyExplanation: Indices are reciprocals of intercepts, so a smaller intercept gives a larger index.
questions.concise: Indices are reciprocals of intercepts, so a smaller intercept ⇒ a larger index.
questions.detailed:
Miller indices are the *reciprocals* of the axial intercepts. Therefore:
```
larger intercept  →  smaller index
smaller intercept →  larger index
```
The plane (201) cuts x at ½, whereas (100) cuts x at 1. Because ½ < 1, its reciprocal 2 > 1.
- (b) is the direct opposite of the truth.
- (c) and (d) are false — indices *are* related to intercepts, reciprocally.
This is the conceptual key to not "reducing" indices wrongly (the Q28 trap).

questions.text: All parallel planes share the same Miller indices; (hkl) denotes one specific set of parallel planes, while {hkl} denotes the whole symmetry-equivalent family.
questions.keyExplanation: True as stated.
questions.concise: (hkl) = one parallel set; {hkl} = the whole symmetry-equivalent family.
questions.detailed:
Correct as stated. All parallel planes share the same Miller indices (hkl); the
braces {hkl} denote the complete set of planes that the symmetry operations map onto each other.

questions.text: The direction [1̄10] has a bar over the first index because:
questions.keyExplanation: The bar denotes a negative component.
questions.concise: The bar denotes a negative index/component.
questions.detailed:
In [1̄10], the bar over the first index means the direction has a negative component
along the x-axis. Bars are used because a minus sign inside brackets would be ambiguous.
- (c) "close-packed direction" is unrelated to the bar.
- (d) Family notation uses angle brackets ⟨uvw⟩, not bars.

questions.text: In a cubic crystal, the interplanar spacing d_hkl is:
questions.keyExplanation: d_hkl = a/√(h²+k²+l²) (cubic).
questions.concise: Cubic: d_hkl = a/√(h²+k²+l²).
questions.detailed:
For any cubic crystal:
```
d_hkl = a / √(h² + k² + l²)
```
- (a) is the reciprocal form (would give a length larger for *smaller* indices — wrong).
- (c) lacks the square root.
- (d) is not the formula.
Larger spacing ⇒ fewer bonds per unit area across the gap ⇒ weaker interplanar bonding —
which is the second half of why the widest-spaced planes slip most easily.

questions.text: For FCC with a = 2√2 R, d₁₁₁ equals (numerically, in units of R):
questions.detailed:
```
d₁₁₁ = a / √(1²+1²+1²) = a/√3
substitute a = 2√2 R:
d₁₁₁ = 2√2 R / √3 = (2 × 1.414)/1.732 R = 2.828/1.732 R ≈ 1.633 R
```
- (a) 1.414 R = √2 R (the FCC face-diagonal/R factor, a distractor).
- (c) 1.732 R = √3 R.
- (d) 2.000 R.
**Note the coincidence:** this equals HCP's ideal c/a (1.633) — same number, unrelated origin,
as your notes warn. Do not conclude the structures are related.

questions.text: For BCC with a = 4R/√3, d₁₁₀ equals (numerically, in units of R):
questions.detailed:
```
d₁₁₀ = a / √(1²+1²+0²) = a/√2
substitute a = 4R/√3:
d₁₁₀ = (4R/√3)/√2 = 4R/(1.732 × 1.414) = 4R/2.449 ≈ 1.633 R
```
- (a) 1.225 R, (b) 1.414 R, (d) 2.309 R are all wrong.
Q33 and Q34 both give 1.633 R — a genuine numerical coincidence your notes explicitly flag as
easy to misremember as connected (see Q37).

questions.text: Slip occurs preferentially on the most densely packed planes and along the most densely packed directions because:

statements.text: close-packed planes have the largest interplanar spacing (easiest to shear)
close-packed directions have the shortest atomic repeat distance (smallest Burgers vector, lowest strain energy)
close-packed planes have the highest atomic packing factor
close-packed planes have the lowest surface energy

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1 and 2 are the reasons. Item 3 is a *restatement* of packing, not the slip mechanism per se; item 4 is not the stated reason.
questions.concise: Slip favours close-packed planes (largest d-spacing) and directions (shortest repeat distance); the APF is a restatement, not the mechanism.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: close-packed planes have the largest interplanar spacing, so are easiest to shear.
- Item 2 — TRUE: close-packed directions have the shortest atomic repeat distance, giving the
  smallest Burgers vector and lowest strain energy (E ∝ b², Ch. 5).
- Item 3 — restates that the plane is close-packed; it is not an *independent* reason why slip
  occurs there. The mechanistic reasons are items 1 and 2.
- Item 4 — surface energy is not the stated reason for slip-plane selection.
The examinable point is the *pair* (largest d-spacing + shortest repeat distance).

questions.text: Linear density is defined as:

options.label: a
options.text: number of atom centres per unit length along a direction

options.label: b
options.text: number of atoms per unit cell

options.label: c
options.text: fraction of volume occupied by atoms

options.label: d
options.text: number of atoms per unit area on a plane

questions.keyExplanation: Atom centres per unit length along a direction.
questions.concise: Linear density = atom centres per unit length along a direction.
questions.detailed:
Linear density counts how many atom centres lie on a unit length of a given
direction — the maximum is 1, attained for a close-packed direction.
- (b) atoms per unit cell — that is the "n" in APF.
- (c) fraction of volume occupied — that is the *atomic packing factor*.
- (d) atoms per unit area — that is the *planar density*.
Three related but distinct density measures; a [P2] trio.

questions.text: Expressed in units of the atomic radius R, FCC's d₁₁₁ and BCC's d₁₁₀ both come out to ≈ 1.633 R. The correct interpretation is:

options.label: a
options.text: therefore FCC and BCC have identical ductility

options.label: b
options.text: the spacings coincide numerically, but FCC has four equivalent {111} planes while BCC's {110} is only the best of several close-competing families — so FCC is far more ductile

options.label: c
options.text: therefore BCC has more slip systems than FCC

options.label: d
options.text: the numbers are identical because both structures are close-packed

questions.keyExplanation: The coincidence is numerical only; the *number of equivalent planes* is what governs ductility.
questions.concise: The 1.633 R coincidence is numerical only; the *number of equivalent planes* governs ductility.
questions.detailed:
Q33 and Q34 showed d₁₁₁(FCC) and d₁₁₀(BCC) both come out to 1.633 R. But:
- FCC has **four** equivalent {111} close-packed planes (from ABCABC stacking), giving 12 slip systems.
- BCC has **no** truly close-packed plane; {110} is merely the best of several close-competing
  families ({110}, {112}, {123}), and it is harder to activate.

So the ductility difference comes from the *count and character* of the slip systems, not from
the interplanar spacing.
- (a), (c), (d) all wrongly infer structural equivalence from the numerical coincidence.

questions.text: In FCC, the octahedral void (r_void/R = 0.414) is located at:

options.label: a
options.text: the body centre and the edge centres

questions.keyExplanation: FCC octahedral voids at body centre (½,½,½) and edge centres (½,0,0).
questions.concise: FCC octahedral voids at (½,½,½) and the 12 edge centres; r_void/R = 0.414.
questions.detailed:
In FCC the octahedral sites are at:
```
body centre:   (½, ½, ½)          → 1
edge centres:  (½,0,0) and perms  → 12 × ¼ = 3
total = 4 octahedral voids per unit cell
```
Each is surrounded by 6 atoms in an octahedron, and r_void/R = √2 − 1 = 0.414.
- (c) (¼,¼,¼) positions are the *tetrahedral* voids (Q39).

questions.text: In FCC, tetrahedral voids of r_void/R = 0.225 occur at the (¼, ¼, ¼)-type positions, and there are how many per unit cell?
questions.keyExplanation: 8 tetrahedral voids per FCC cell at (¼,¼,¼)-type positions.
questions.concise: FCC has 8 tetrahedral voids per cell at (¼,¼,¼)-type positions.
questions.detailed:
The tetrahedral voids sit at (¼,¼,¼) and all symmetry-equivalent positions —
including (¾,¾,¼) etc. — giving **8 per unit cell**, each surrounded by 4 atoms, with
r_void/R = √6/2 − 1 = 0.225.
- (a) 4 is the number of octahedral voids in FCC (Q38).
- (b) 6 is the number of FCC atoms/cell... no, FCC has 4 atoms; 6 is the number of faces.
- (d) 12 is the FCC coordination number.
The 8-vs-4 void count (tetrahedral vs octahedral in FCC) is worth pairing.

questions.text: In BCC, which void is *nominally* larger?
questions.keyExplanation: BCC tetrahedral 0.291 > octahedral 0.155. [P2] — note the **reversal** vs FCC, where octahedral (0.414) is the larger.
questions.concise: In BCC the tetrahedral void (0.291) is nominally larger than the octahedral (0.155).
questions.detailed:
```
BCC octahedral void:  r_void/R = 2/√3 − 1 = 0.155
BCC tetrahedral void: r_void/R = 0.291
```
So in BCC, **tetrahedral > octahedral**.
**This is the exact reverse of FCC**, where octahedral (0.414) > tetrahedral (0.225).
This reversal is precisely the [P2] paired-terminology trap — students assume "octahedral is
always the bigger void" from the FCC case. Hold the two side by side:
| | larger void |
|---|---|
| FCC | octahedral (0.414) |
| BCC | tetrahedral (0.291) |
And then see Q41 for the twist that carbon ignores this.

questions.assertion: Carbon in ferrite (BCC α-Fe) occupies the *octahedral* site even though the BCC tetrahedral void is nominally larger.
questions.reason: The BCC octahedral void is strongly anisotropic — its two nearest neighbours sit far closer than its four next-nearest neighbours — so an interstitial there pushes on only two atoms rather than distorting four more symmetrically.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true and R correctly explains A — this anisotropy is exactly why C sits in the *smaller* site and why martensite is tetragonal.
questions.concise: The BCC octahedral site is anisotropic (2 close neighbours, not 4), so carbon sits there despite it being nominally smaller.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: carbon in ferrite occupies the *octahedral* site even though the BCC tetrahedral
  void is nominally larger (0.291 > 0.155).
- R is TRUE: the BCC octahedral site is strongly anisotropic — its two nearest neighbours sit
  far closer than its four next-nearest neighbours. An interstitial there therefore pushes on
  only two atoms rather than distorting four more symmetrically.

R correctly explains A: the *shape* of the distortion, not the nominal radius, decides where
carbon sits. Because the distortion is strongly directional along ⟨100⟩, this also explains
why carbon-supersaturated martensite becomes **tetragonal** (Q44). This is one of the most
examinable ideas in Ch. 2 — the nominal-size intuition is deliberately wrong.

questions.text: From Leslie's data, the octahedral void radii in FCC austenite and BCC ferrite are respectively:
questions.keyExplanation: FCC austenite octahedral 0.052 nm; BCC ferrite octahedral 0.019 nm.
questions.concise: FCC austenite octahedral void 0.052 nm; BCC ferrite octahedral void 0.019 nm.
questions.detailed:
From Leslie's data as given in your Ch. 2 notes:
```
FCC austenite (γ-Fe) octahedral void:  0.052 nm
BCC ferrite   (α-Fe) octahedral void:  0.019 nm
```
The FCC void is nearly **three times larger** — which is exactly why austenite dissolves far
more carbon (up to ~2.1 wt%) than ferrite (~0.022 wt%), and why quenching traps carbon to form
martensite. Options (b), (c), (d) all either swap the two or invent a third value.

questions.text: The carbon atom radius is ≈ 0.08 nm, which is:

options.label: a
options.text: smaller than every void in both structures

options.label: b
options.text: larger than every void in both structures — so dissolving carbon always costs lattice strain energy

options.label: c
options.text: exactly equal to the FCC octahedral void radius

options.label: d
options.text: smaller than the BCC octahedral void

questions.keyExplanation: C (0.08 nm) exceeds both, so dissolution always costs strain energy.
questions.concise: C (0.08 nm) exceeds every void, so dissolution always costs strain energy.
questions.detailed:
```
Carbon atom radius:        0.08 nm
FCC austenite octahedral:  0.052 nm
BCC ferrite octahedral:    0.019 nm
BCC tetrahedral:           ~0.036 nm
```
Carbon (0.08 nm) is **larger than every available void**, so it never fits comfortably — it
always distorts the lattice and costs strain energy. That strain energy is precisely the origin
of **solid-solution strengthening** (Ch. 7) and, when many carbon atoms sit on one ⟨100⟩ axis,
of **martensite tetragonality** (Q44).
- (a) and (d) claim C fits inside a void — false.
- (c) is not the correct pairing.

questions.text: The tetragonality of carbon-supersaturated martensite follows:
questions.keyExplanation: c/a = 1.000 + 0.045 (wt% C); distortion measurable beyond ≈0.20 wt% C.
questions.concise: Martensite tetragonality: c/a = 1.000 + 0.045 × (wt% C).
questions.detailed:
In carbon-supersaturated martensite, carbon preferentially occupies octahedral sites
along *one* ⟨100⟩ axis, stretching that axis:
```
c/a = 1.000 + 0.045 (wt% C)
```
- At 0 wt% C, c/a = 1.000 (cubic).
- Each 1 wt% C raises c/a by 0.045.
The distortion becomes measurable above ~0.20 wt% C. The cell is therefore body-centred
**tetragonal** (BCT), not cubic.
- (b) wrongly starts from the HCP ideal 1.633.
- (c) has the wrong sign (would *compress* c).
- (d) omits the 1.000 baseline entirely.

questions.text: Why does carbon dissolve far more readily in austenite (γ-Fe, FCC, up to ≈2.1 wt%) than in ferrite (α-Fe, BCC, ≈0.022 wt%)?

statements.text: FCC has the *larger* octahedral void (0.052 nm vs 0.019 nm).
BCC has the lower packing factor overall, yet its voids are individually smaller.
The carbon atom is larger than both voids, so the larger void costs less strain energy.
FCC has a lower melting point than BCC.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is irrelevant/false as a cause.
questions.concise: FCC has the larger void; BCC's overall APF is lower but its individual voids are smaller; C exceeds both so the larger void costs less strain. Melting point is irrelevant.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: FCC octahedral void 0.052 nm > BCC octahedral 0.019 nm (Q42).
- Item 2 — TRUE: BCC has lower *overall* APF (0.68 vs 0.74), yet its *individual* voids are
  smaller — a genuinely counter-intuitive point that examiners love.
- Item 3 — TRUE: carbon (0.08 nm) is larger than both, so the larger void imposes less strain
  energy; FCC is therefore the roomier host.
- Item 4 — FALSE: melting point is not the cause (and FCC γ-Fe is not simply lower-melting in
  the relevant sense). This is the invented distractor that kills the "all" option.
This question ties together Q38–Q44 into one coherent picture: **larger voids, more C, and the
BCC/FCC solubility difference that drives all of steel heat treatment.**

questions.text: The correct sequence of iron allotropes on heating is:
questions.keyExplanation: α (BCC) →912→ γ (FCC) →1394→ δ (BCC) →1538→ liquid.
questions.concise: α BCC → γ FCC → δ BCC → liquid.
questions.detailed:
On heating iron:
```
α-Fe (BCC)  --912 °C-->  γ-Fe (FCC, austenite)
γ-Fe (FCC)  --1394 °C--> δ-Fe (BCC)
δ-Fe (BCC)  --1538 °C--> liquid
```
- (b) reverses the α/γ order.
- (c) swaps the 912 and 1394 °C temperatures.
- (d) puts δ at the wrong end.
The pattern to note: BCC → FCC → **BCC** → liquid. Iron is BCC at both the lowest and the
highest solid temperatures, and FCC (austenite) only in between. This is the physical basis of
every steel heat treatment.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true of the BCC↔FCC transformation in iron?

statements.text: It is the physical basis of all steel heat treatment (austenitizing, quenching, tempering).
Carbon solubility differs drastically between α (≈0.022 wt%) and γ (≈2.1 wt% at 1148 °C).
γ-Fe is FCC and is called austenite.
δ-Fe is FCC.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is **false** — δ-Fe is BCC, not FCC. [P1]
questions.concise: The α↔γ transformation underpins steel heat treatment; C solubility differs drastically; γ-Fe is austenite — but δ-Fe is BCC, not FCC.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: this transformation is the basis of austenitizing, quenching, tempering.
- Item 2 — TRUE: α ≈ 0.022 wt% C vs γ ≈ 2.1 wt% at 1148 °C — a ~100× difference.
- Item 3 — TRUE: γ-Fe is FCC and is called austenite.
- Item 4 — FALSE: δ-Fe is **BCC**, not FCC. (Your course materials quote the γ max C as
  2.06–2.11 wt%; the point stands either way.)
The false member is a single structural mis-assignment — exactly the P1 shape where one
quietly-wrong item defeats an otherwise-correct list.

questions.assertion: Quenching austenite rapidly traps carbon and produces the hard, brittle phase martensite.
questions.reason: Carbon is far more soluble in FCC austenite than in BCC ferrite, and rapid cooling gives no time for that carbon to precipitate or diffuse out.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true; the solubility difference + no time to diffuse is precisely why quenching traps carbon.
questions.concise: Carbon is far more soluble in FCC austenite; rapid cooling gives no time for it to precipitate, so it is trapped as martensite.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: quenching austenite rapidly traps carbon and forms hard, brittle martensite.
- R is TRUE: carbon is far more soluble in FCC austenite (~2.1 wt%) than in BCC ferrite
  (~0.022 wt%), and rapid cooling gives no time for that carbon to precipitate or diffuse out.

R correctly explains A. The mechanism chain: austenitize (dissolve C in FCC) → quench (no time
for diffusion) → carbon stays in solution → the FCC→BCT shear transformation drags the carbon
with it → tetragonal, supersaturated, hard martensite. This is the single most important
practical consequence in the whole of Ch. 2.

questions.text: For Bragg's law, if the interplanar spacing for (111) in a cubic crystal is $d_{111}=0.200\,\text{nm}$ and the X-ray wavelength is $\lambda=0.154\,\text{nm}$, the first-order ($n=1$) diffraction angle $2\theta$ is approximately:
questions.keyExplanation: $n\lambda=2d\sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \lambda/(2d)=0.154/(0.400)=0.385 \Rightarrow \theta=22.6^\circ \Rightarrow 2\theta=45.2^\circ$.
questions.concise: $\sin\theta = \lambda/(2d)=0.154/0.400=0.385 \Rightarrow \theta=22.6^\circ \Rightarrow 2\theta=45.2^\circ$.
questions.detailed:
$$
n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta \implies \sin\theta = \frac{n\lambda}{2d} = \frac{0.154\,\text{nm}}{0.400\,\text{nm}} = 0.385 \implies \theta \approx 22.6^\circ.
$$
Thus $2\theta \approx 45.2^\circ$.

questions.text: In Bragg's law $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$, the factor $2d$ appears because:

options.label: a
options.text: X-rays are reflected from two parallel planes separated by distance $d$

options.label: d
options.text: both incident and scattered beams are considered separately

questions.keyExplanation: Bragg's condition gives constructive interference from reflections off two parallel planes separated by $d$.
questions.concise: The path difference between rays reflected from adjacent parallel planes is $2d\sin\theta$.
questions.detailed:
For two parallel planes distance $d$ apart, the lower ray travels an extra path $2d\sin\theta$
relative to the upper; constructive interference occurs when that equals $n\lambda$. Hence the $2d$ factor.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about carbon in iron and its interstitial voids is/are correct?

statements.text: Austenite (FCC) has a larger octahedral void radius (≈0.052 nm) than ferrite (BCC) (≈0.019 nm).
The carbon atom (≈0.08 nm) is larger than the octahedral voids in both structures.
Even though BCC has a larger tetrahedral void (0.291 R vs 0.155 R), carbon prefers the BCC octahedral site because of the strong anisotropy of that site.
Austenite dissolves far more carbon than ferrite mainly because the strain energy penalty of putting C into its larger octahedral void is much smaller.

questions.keyExplanation: All 1–4 are correct — larger FCC octahedral void + small C size => much lower strain energy penalty in austenite.
questions.concise: Larger FCC octahedral void + C (0.08 nm) exceeds voids in both, but the strain-energy penalty is far smaller in FCC austenite, so more C dissolves.
questions.detailed:
- 1 TRUE: FCC austenite octahedral ≈ 0.052 nm, BCC ferrite ≈ 0.019 nm.
- 2 TRUE: C ≈ 0.08 nm exceeds both octahedral voids.
- 3 TRUE: BCC tetrahedral (0.291 R) is larger than octahedral (0.155 R), but strong anisotropy of
  the BCC octahedral site means C actually prefers the octahedral site despite the tetrahedral being
  "nominally" larger — a well-known point.
- 4 TRUE: The key to carbon solubility difference is the much smaller strain-energy penalty in the
  larger FCC octahedral void.

questions.text: Despite having the same atomic packing factor (0.74), HCP polycrystals are generally less ductile than FCC polycrystals because:

options.label: a
options.text: HCP provides only about 3 independent basal slip systems, whereas FCC provides ≥ 5 independent systems

options.label: b
options.text: HCP has fewer atoms per unit cell than FCC

options.label: c
options.text: the metallic bond is stronger in HCP

options.label: d
options.text: HCP has a lower melting point

questions.keyExplanation: Von Mises requires ≥5 independent slip systems for polycrystal deformation; HCP basal gives only ~3 independent, so less ductile despite same APF.
questions.concise: Von Mises requires ≥5 independent slip systems for homogeneous polycrystal deformation; HCP has only ~3, so less ductile despite identical APF.
questions.detailed:
Identical packing density doesn't ensure equal ductility. HCP's primary (0001)⟨112̄0⟩ basal
systems give only 3 independent systems; FCC gives 12 total but more directly ≥5 independent systems
are available, satisfying the von Mises criterion for polycrystals.

questions.text: Two structures have $d_{111}(\text{FCC}) \approx 1.633\,R$ and $d_{110}(\text{BCC}) \approx 1.633\,R$ (numerically identical). The correct metallurgical interpretation is:

options.label: a
options.text: FCC and BCC must have identical ductility

options.label: b
options.text: the number of equivalent close-packed slip planes differs greatly — FCC has four equivalent {111} planes while BCC slips on several families — so packing-factor identity does not imply equal ductility

options.label: c
options.text: this means BCC has more slip systems than FCC

options.label: d
options.text: it follows because both are close-packed structures

questions.keyExplanation: Identical numerical spacing doesn't imply equal ductility; the *number of equivalent close-packed planes* and independent systems differs. FCC has four {111} families vs BCC's multiple active families.
questions.concise: Numerical spacing equality is a coincidence; slip-system multiplicity (number of equivalent close-packed planes/families and independent systems) governs ductility.
questions.detailed:
Both give $d \approx 1.633R$ numerically, but ductility depends on available slip systems.
FCC has four equivalent {111} planes; BCC has no truly close-packed plane and slips on {110}/{112}/{123}
families depending on T. The "three families give 48 total" helps, but the *equivalent close-packed
plane count* difference is the point here.
